title: Beige Book — September 3, 2025
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2025-09-03 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Most Districts reported little or no change; four reported modest growth. Data center construction was a rare bright spot in commercial real estate. Manufacturers shifted toward local suppliers where possible and added automation to cut costs. Sentiment was mixed, with economic uncertainty and tariffs the most frequently cited negatives. The report was prepared by the Philadelphia Fed.

Consumer spending

Flat to declining, as wages lagged rising prices. New York noted consumers "squeezed by rising costs of insurance, utilities, and other expenses." Retailers and hotels offered deals to keep price-sensitive shoppers. Domestic leisure travel held up while international visitors fell. Auto sales were flat to slightly higher, with more demand for repairs on older vehicles.

Labor markets

Eleven Districts reported little or no net change in employment. Seven said firms were hesitant to hire, and layoffs rose in two. Several reported headcount cuts through attrition, helped by return-to-office policies and automation, including AI tools. Most Districts saw more job seekers. Half reported a reduced supply of immigrant labor. Wage growth was modest in half the Districts, moderate in most others.

Prices

Ten Districts described price growth as moderate or modest; two said input price growth was strong and outpaced selling prices. Nearly all cited tariff-related increases, especially on inputs; insurance, utilities and technology services also rose. Many firms hesitated to pass costs along; Cleveland and Minneapolis reported pressure to cut prices. Most Districts expected continued increases, and three expected the pace to accelerate.

Notable themes

  • AI/data centers: AI deployment partly explained data center construction (Philadelphia, Cleveland, Chicago) and higher energy demand (Atlanta, Kansas City).
  • Tariffs: Most cited factor for costs and uncertainty.
  • Immigration: Construction labor hit in New York, Richmond, St. Louis and San Francisco.
  • Consumer squeeze: Wages lagging prices.

District highlights

  • Philadelphia: Modest growth; tariffs and federal budget cuts expected to add stress.
  • Chicago: Modest growth with moderate consumer spending gains.
  • New York: Slight decline tied to tariff uncertainty; strong input price growth.
  • Minneapolis: Slight contraction; weak agriculture on poor commodity prices despite good crops.
  • Kansas City: Profit margins declined.
  • St. Louis: Slightly pessimistic, though deterioration eased; expects tariffs to raise prices over the next year.
  • Dallas: Outlooks improved, but worries about trade policy, high interest rates and immigration.

Read-through for SPY

  • Stagnant activity and squeezed consumers argued for caution on consumer discretionary names.
  • The AI/data center build-out stood out as a growth driver, supportive of tech and related infrastructure.
  • Soft hiring plus sticky tariff inflation left the Fed balancing a cooling labor market against prices.
